thread.title: Gifts to help people unplug and get back to a life before smartphones

author: Andrew Keshner
title: Gifts to help people unplug and get back to a life before smartphones
text:
This story is part of a MarketWatch series, “ Gifts that pay off ,” about presents that have a larger impact long after the holiday season has passed.
In today’s hyper-connected world, some people feel like they’re so tethered to their devices that they’ve forgotten how to live in the moment.
This holiday season, why not give the present of helping others be present? After all, all that online shopping adds up. Cyber Monday , the day when people shop online to kick off the holiday season, was the biggest U.S. online shopping day in history. People spent $7.9 billion on that day this year, a 20% increase on the year before.
There are all kinds of gifts and experiences that can promote that old-school, unplugged state of mind and help people get unglued from their screens. It could be a game, an outing, breaking bread together or something else altogether, experts told MarketWatch. But there was a common thread that ran through it all — a shared activity that requires people to be in the moment.
There are all kinds of gifts and experiences that can promote that old-school, unplugged state of mind and help people stop spending so much time and money on their screens. A growing body of research has said constantly being hooked to our phones is taking a toll on us humans. Research released earlier this month claimed to the first to find a causal link between Facebook FB, -0.08% use and depression. That particular study was published in the December peer-reviewed Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology
Maybe the growing awareness that our phones could be zapping our mental health has something to do with Vitamin Water’s KO, -0.86% recent announcement that it would pay $100,000 to someone who can ditch their smartphone for a year. But you don’t need to be a lucky contest winner to pry yourself away from your smartphone.
Emily Mackie, the founder and owner of Inspired Interiors, a Chicago, Ill.-based interior design firm, suggested buying a classic game of darts. The good news: There are all prices of dartboards to choose from; prices can be as low as $15, though more elaborate versions made of wood with scoreboards attached can cost $100 or more.
Years ago, Mackie’s father converted the family basement into a full-fledged game room, replete with arcade games, a pool table and a dart board.
She remembered good times throwing darts, either while sipping hot chocolate as kid or having a beer as a young adult. “It was a great time to goof off and have conversation,” said Mackie.
Choose from a myriad of board games or, for those who don’t want to commit to one game until they’ve tried it out, board game subscription services, some of which cost up to $50 a month. Mackie’s dart board suggestion would go a long way to recreate a time when families played games together instead of sticking their noses in their iPhones AAPL, -2.11% buying stuff they may not even need.
For people worried about marking the walls, Mackie suggested buying some cheap foam padding as protection. Mackie doesn’t have a dart board at the moment, because one of her kids is 6, she said. But a set of Nerf guns that she occasionally uses to run around with her kids works as an alternative.
Other time-tested, unplugged fun includes bocce ball ($99 for a set) and dominoes ( just $11.99 for a "designer” version ).There are, of course, a myriad of board games to choose from and, for those who don’t want to commit to one game until they’ve tried it out, board game subscription services, some of which cost up to $50 a month. (Read more about those subscription services here .
Board games are an obvious way to bring the family together over Christmas. Balderdash ($15 on Amazon AMZN, -2.28% ), a quirky trivia game, is designed to puzzle adults as much as children by asking quirky questions that require everyone to use their imagination to both suggest and guess the right answer. The beauty for children who play: sometimes the wildest, most unexpected answer is the correct one.
Try a ‘conversation pit’ or a hot pot Mackie’s day job now involves creating “communal spaces” at home and at work. It’s possible to give the gift of space for, well, connecting to each other instead of machines. In fact, the “conversation pit,” a room’s delightful divot devoted to chit-chat, is reportedly making a bit of a comeback after being out of style for a few decades, at least according to some interior design blogs.
Here’s the good news: You can achieve the sunken look without a massive renovation, New York magazine reported. Want to help someone get started with a holiday gift? Try a couple of floor pillows at $50 each.
There are other gifts to help people be in the moment, and they don’t involve games of skill and luck or a home redesign.
“Bring back the fondue set,” Mackie said. She uses her set for dessert and has discovered that it has the side effect of lengthening conversations, especially with her kids. “A big bowl of hot melted chocolate will kind of keep them at the table a little while,” Mackie said. Many fondue sets cost between $50 and $100.
Along those lines, Robin Haas, a Boston, Mass. life coach, said she loved her hot pot, where shabu shabu dishes — the dipping of proteins and vegetables in broth — become more flavorful. The kitchen gadgets also help cook up social interactions by drawing people together around the pot. “You’re all working together to create this really fun meal,” Haas said. Pots for these meals can cost around $50. Slow cookers can also be used this way.
Then there are gifts to help to foster cooking — which can be an engaging group activity — without the hassle of ingredient shopping and menu research. Two recipes for a four-person meal costs just over $70 at Blue Apron , which delivers the ingredients and recipes.
Other ways to promote IRL (‘in real life’) togetherness this holiday season? Have a Christmas tree ornament party or a group art project, or even gift your loved one with a craft maker. Other ways to promote IRL (“in real life”) togetherness this holiday season? Have a Christmas tree ornament party or a group art project.
You can even buy sophisticated gadgets that will help your loved ones become more crafty: The Cricut Explore Air 2 sells for around $199 and its professional grade machine, the Cricut Maker, sells for $349. The Silhouette Cameo 3 retails for $299. Other brands include Brother, with its Designncut ($199) or Cm350 ($299) machines, and Artistic Edge ($299). As this MarketWatch article points out , it may encourage the receiver of the gift to start their own side hustle on Etsy ETSY, -4.25%
To give the gift of experiences — which have been shown to make us happier than material possessions — try museum passes or tickets to a special event, Haas noted. Sites like Viator.com list activities in all sorts of places. Meanwhile, the National Park Service sells “ America the Beautiful Passes ,” which let holders skip ticket lines at more than 2,000 federal recreation sites. They cost $80 yearly for adults and $20 for seniors.
Here’s one that costs nothing, but promotes interest in literature, which some academics would argue is priceless. This particular game requires plucking random books from a person’s living room. Each person guesses the first line by reading the book jacket. Then the suggested first lines are read one by one, and the person who guesses the correct first line wins. Often times, the creative versions that were dreamed up by the participants are even more arresting than the actual first line of the book’s Chapter 1.
But unplugging and truly connecting don’t have to cost anything, Haas said. It could be as simple as talking. ”I’m of the belief that with every conversation… We get a little closer to world peace.”
(Quentin Fottrell contributed to this story.)
